text: Two tyres roll over the same nail. One goes flat in seconds. The other keeps going for miles. To see why, we have to cut them open.
This is a tube tyre. Slice a piece away, and look closely. There are three layers. The metal rim. The black tyre. And hidden inside, a second ring of soft rubber. The inner tube.
The tube is basically a balloon, bent into a ring. Its valve pokes out through a small hole in the rim. That's where you pump.
Watch the air go in. It fills the tube, and the tube swells, until it presses hard against the inside of the tyre, all the way round.
So the tyre itself holds no air at all. It's a tough shell that grips the road, while the tube holds the pressure.
Now the tubeless tyre. Same slice. Rim. Tyre. And... no tube! The air sits directly inside the tyre.
To keep it in, the inside of the tyre is coated with a special airtight rubber. And this rim has no spoke holes, so the metal is sealed too.
The clever part is the edges. Each one hides a ring of steel wire, called the bead. Pump in air, and the pressure shoves both beads outwards, until they snap onto the rim. Pop!
Now the tyre and the rim make one sealed chamber. And the more air you add, the harder the beads press, and the tighter it seals.
Now, the nail. It punches through the tyre, and straight into the tube. And stretched rubber can't hold a hole shut. It pulls it wide open.
The air rushes out, slips between the tube and the tyre, and escapes through the holes in the rim. In seconds, the tyre collapses.
In the tubeless tyre, nothing is stretched. The nail sits in thick rubber, and the rubber squeezes tightly around it. Like a cork.
Only a little air hisses out, very slowly. Often slow enough to ride on to a repair shop.
Fixing them is different too. A tube tyre has to come off the rim, so you can pull the tube out and patch it.
The tubeless one? Pull out the nail, and push a sticky rubber plug in from outside. Done in minutes.
And with no tube rubbing inside, a tubeless tyre runs cooler, and it's often a little lighter.
So why do tubes still exist? A wire spoke wheel has a hole for every spoke, and the air would leak right out. So most of them need a tube. Tubes are also cheap, and easy to swap anywhere.
For everyday roads, tubeless wins. Not because it never gets a puncture. But because when it does, it fails slowly. And slow is safe.
Orbi Transfer was built the same way. Nothing extra in the middle. No login, no app. Your file is sealed on your own phone, before it ever leaves.
It appears on the other screen in about a second. And after thirty minutes, it's gone.
Orbi Transfer dot com. Same nail. Very different ending.
